Two things really.

That you might be a human being and thus biased. Consider politely asking people what they believe and why. Don't even need to really argue with them just ask if they have any interesting sources as your digging may be biased.

The gellman effect.

"Briefly stated, the Gell-Mann Amnesia effect works as follows. You open the newspaper to an article on some subject you know well. In Murray’s case, physics. In mine, show business. You read the article and see the journalist has absolutely no understanding of either the facts or the issues. Often, the article is so wrong it actually presents the story backward-reversing cause and effect. I call these the “wet streets cause rain” stories. Paper’s full of them.

In any case, you read with exasperation or amusement the multiple errors in a story-and then turn the page to national or international affairs, and read with renewed interest as if the rest of the newspaper was somehow more accurate about far-off Palestine than it was about the story you just read. You turn the page, and forget what you know."

To summarize do not trust newspapers unless you have a really good reason to do so.

there are some works that you have to do with robot on. the robots we have have key switch "manual 100%" that lets you run robot full speed from teach pendant (you have to keep deadmans switch pressed on teach pendant). in that mode some safety systems (gates, light fences) are bypassed.

I was surprised, that it happened in Germany, because as far as i know, they have pretty strict safety rules. Robots themselves (ABBs and fanucs, that i have experience with) have very good safety systems internally - 2 channel safety chain goes through every block and if any of them fail, it all defaults to no-go and E-stop is engaged, robot arm de-energised and put to brake.

Of course there was lot of comments about AI taking over and difference of human and car (think of "how robot can mix up human and car? they are nothing alike") but truth is, that most of industrial robotics have no need for any sort of AI and programming is very linear.
Don't they have laser fences around them?

usually they have laser fences and/or physical fence and gate. they are usually routed via general stop or autostop chain, so manual robot functions are availible even if gate is opened or lightfence broken.

i have no information, what really happened, but my guess would be that they set the robot on automatic mode on purpose (it is doable if there is someone to help you do that outside the cell) to test something or something similar.

If a machine malfunctions, do you shut it down to repair parts or just swap it out with a new one?

Also, what kind of MTTF are we talking about here? Which machines tend to malfunction the most?

"industry standard" is to turn it off, and replace failed part. mostly with robots, it's external things that fail - light fences, sensors, cables. lot of those get repaired within hour (and is reason, why the company employs me inhouse instead of on call) in lot of other machines (milling, lathes routing tables) servo drives are common failure.
Just looked up ABB robotics (didn't know if it was a company or type of robot). What's the most common thing to fail on one of these?

mechanicly on smaller robots - wrists. even when loaded according to specifications, with time they start to have free-movement, and have to be changed, if you want precision. electrically - servo drives on older robots.

lot of problems are not with robots themselves, but all the peripherials - turning tables, sensors, cables.

Interesting! Out of curiosity, what do you consider to be a smaller robot? ABB has everything from robots that handle payloads of 600 kg down to 500 g. Can you say which type you use at the company and what kinds of things they do?

oldest we have are irb2000, most of robots are IRB2400 (and some other, but mostly they are pretty much the same as 2400) we use them for welding MIG, TIG, plasma - you can get the process much more consistent that with human welder and operators (who place pieces in and out of jig) don't have to be welders. also few of robots handle parts with press-brakes - it is bit slower than human operator, but then again one operator can work on 4 stations (mostly loading parts in magazine and changing pallets with bent pieces.) we also have robot doing the same with grinding stations.
How frequently the industrial robots goes wrong?

some robots are from hell - there is allways something wrong with them, but some go for years without much attention. most often it is external things, not robots themselves - lightfences, sensors, cabling. if we take just robots i'd say i do actual repairs on robots 2-3 times a year. some minor problems occur more often, but thy could be fixed by operator guided on phone.
